transcript.text: Our Henry has gone a bit weak and sounds rough, sort of rattly growl instead of the normal hum. It's about 12 years old. Bags and filter are new. Worth fixing?

It may well be worth fixing, but not until the airflow path has been ruled out. A 12-year-old Henry-type vacuum is often worth repairing if it is a blockage, floorhead issue or a serviceable motor fault; a motor replacement becomes less attractive if the repair quote is a large proportion of a replacement machine. New bags and filter remove the commonest cause, but weak pickup plus a rattly growl still most often comes down to either:
1. A partial blockage or something rattling/jamming in the hose, floorhead or brush bar.
2. A worn motor bearing/brush or damaged fan — more likely if the rough growl remains with the whole suction route clear. 1. Unplug it. Remove the hose, tubes and floorhead, then look through each section towards a light. Check the floorhead neck and the machine inlet as well. Clear any lodged debris.
2. Turn the floorhead over and remove hair/thread; the brush bar should turn freely by hand and not rattle excessively. If those are completely clear and the noise is still a rough growl, especially if suction directly at the machine inlet is weak, the motor is the likely fault and an appliance repairer can assess it. Don’t keep running it for long if it sounds like grinding, as a failing bearing or fan can worsen quickly.
[Helpful to see: image "Poor suction — what to check first" — Lost suction is usually a full bin, a dirty filter or a blockage in the hose, tube or floor head — check and clear those before suspecting the motor. Switch off and unplug first. Typical layout — your model may differ.]

Thank you. I've checked the hose and a coin drops straight through, and the suction is weak at both the hose end and the head. I should also mention that after about five minutes it gives off a hot, burning electrical smell, and in a dark hall I saw what looked like sparks flickering inside the top grille. Is that important?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Yes — that is very important. Do not use it again. A hot burning electrical smell and visible flickering/sparking, together with the rough growl and weak suction, point to a failing motor, most commonly worn carbon brushes, damaged bearings or armature damage. With the bag/filter renewed and the hose passing a coin, this is no longer a sensible airflow-only diagnosis. It needs a qualified vacuum repairer to inspect the motor and its wiring; it is not safe to keep testing it or to run it until it fails. At around 12 years old, repair can still be worthwhile if it is brushes or a straightforward motor replacement, but get a quote first: if the total is approaching a substantial fraction of a new Henry, replacement is usually the better value. What are the make and full model number from the rating label, usually on the body or underside? I can then say what repair route is most realistic, without assuming compatibility.
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
Thank you, I'll stop using it. It's a Numatic Henry, and the label on the bottom says HVR 200-22.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
The HVR 200-22 identification supports the same repair route: keep it out of service and have a qualified vacuum repairer inspect the motor assembly and its wiring. The combination of weak suction at the hose, a rough rattly growl, heat/burning smell and flickering visible through the grille makes a failing motor the clear leading cause. The engineer will need to check the carbon brushes and commutator for arcing, the motor bearings for roughness, and the fan/impeller for damage. A simple hose blockage is now much less likely. It is not a part to buy on symptoms alone: worn brushes can sometimes be a viable repair, whereas a scored commutator, damaged fan or worn bearings usually makes a replacement motor the practical option. Given its age, ask for a quote before authorising work; if the all-in repair cost is a substantial proportion of a replacement Henry, replacement is usually better value.
